concepts.name: Kolmogorov Complexity
concepts.definition: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program (in a universal programming language) that outputs the string and then halts.
concepts.intuition: Think of it as the minimum amount of code needed to recreate a piece of data — like describing a picture with the fewest words possible.
concepts.importance: It provides a theoretical foundation for measuring information content independent of probability, forming the basis of algorithmic information theory.
concepts.example: The string '0101010101' has low Kolmogorov complexity because it can be generated by a short program like 'print '01' five times'.

concepts.name: Algorithmic Randomness
concepts.definition: A string is algorithmically random if it has no compressible pattern — its Kolmogorov complexity is approximately equal to its length.
concepts.intuition: Like a truly shuffled deck of cards — no shortcut exists to describe the order; you must list every card.
concepts.importance: It formalizes the intuitive notion of randomness in mathematics, distinguishing true randomness from pseudo-randomness.
concepts.example: A random 1000-bit string generated by a fair coin flip is likely algorithmically random because no program shorter than 1000 bits can reproduce it.

concepts.name: Conditional Complexity
concepts.definition: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string x given another string y as auxiliary information, denoted C(x|y), is the length of the shortest program that outputs x when given y as input.
concepts.intuition: It’s like asking how much extra information you need to rebuild x if you already know y — e.g., how many more facts do you need to describe a car if you already know its make?
concepts.importance: Enables analysis of shared information between objects and underpins mutual information in algorithmic theory.
concepts.example: If y is the first 50 bits of x, then C(x|y) is close to 50 — you only need the second half of x.

concepts.name: Prefix Complexity
concepts.definition: A variant of Kolmogorov complexity where programs are self-delimiting — the machine knows when the program ends without needing a separate end marker.
concepts.intuition: Like writing instructions where each line tells you how long the next one is, so you never get confused about where it ends.
concepts.importance: Avoids ambiguities in program boundaries; essential for defining universal probability and algorithmic randomness rigorously.
concepts.example: The prefix program '01 110' tells the machine: read two bits, then three bits — no need for a stop signal.

concepts.name: Martin-Löf Randomness
concepts.definition: A sequence is Martin-Löf random if it passes all effectively computable statistical tests for randomness — i.e., it does not belong to any recursively enumerable null set.
concepts.intuition: Imagine a casino inspector with an infinite checklist of patterns to detect cheating; if the sequence passes all tests, it’s truly random.
concepts.importance: It is the standard formal definition of randomness in algorithmic information theory and connects to computability theory.
concepts.example: Chaitin’s constant Ω is Martin-Löf random — its bits are unpredictable and incompressible.

concepts.name: Effective Null Sets
concepts.definition: A set of infinite binary sequences that has measure zero and can be effectively enumerated by a computable process.
concepts.intuition: Like a list of all possible 'lucky streaks' in coin flips that are so rare they’ll never happen — and we can write a program to list them all.
concepts.importance: Used to define randomness by excluding 'non-random' patterns that can be algorithmically detected.
concepts.example: The set of all sequences with infinitely many 0s in even positions is an effective null set because we can enumerate violations.

concepts.name: A Priori Probability
concepts.definition: The probability that a universal prefix machine outputs a given string when fed random bits, defined as the sum of 2^(-length(p)) over all programs p that produce the string.
concepts.intuition: It’s the chance a randomly typed program will generate your data — like monkey-typing until it produces Hamlet.
concepts.importance: Provides a universal prior probability distribution over strings, foundational for Bayesian algorithmic inference.
concepts.example: The string '0' has higher a priori probability than '101001010110' because more short programs generate it.

concepts.name: Monotone Complexity
concepts.definition: The length of the shortest monotone program that outputs a string as a prefix — programs can output bits one at a time without backtracking.
concepts.intuition: Like building a string piece by piece, never erasing or revising — each new bit adds to what you already have.
concepts.importance: Connects algorithmic information with probability distributions over infinite sequences and is used in Levin’s theory.
concepts.example: To generate '01', a monotone machine might first output '0', then later output '1' — no need to rewind or overwrite.

concepts.name: Levin-Schnorr Theorem
concepts.definition: A sequence is Martin-Löf random if and only if its prefix complexity at each initial segment n is close to n — specifically, C(x₁…xₙ) ≥ n - c for some constant c.
concepts.intuition: True randomness means you can’t compress the first n bits much — each bit adds nearly one unit of information.
concepts.importance: Bridges Kolmogorov complexity and Martin-Löf randomness, proving they are two sides of the same coin.
concepts.example: For a random sequence, the first 100 bits require nearly 100 bits to describe — no compression possible.

concepts.name: Shannon Entropy
concepts.definition: A measure of average uncertainty or information content in a random variable, calculated as H(X) = -Σ p(x) log p(x).
concepts.intuition: Like measuring how surprised you are on average when you see an outcome — fair coin flips give maximum surprise.
concepts.importance: Foundational in classical information theory; contrasts with Kolmogorov complexity by relying on probability distributions.
concepts.example: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; a biased coin with P(heads)=0.9 has lower entropy because outcomes are more predictable.

concepts.name: Mutual Information (Algorithmic)
concepts.definition: The amount of information shared between two strings x and y, defined as I(x:y) = C(x) + C(y) - C(x,y).
concepts.intuition: How much you can save by describing x and y together instead of separately — like sharing a map to find two locations.
concepts.importance: Quantifies dependency between strings without assuming probability, enabling analysis of data relationships.
concepts.example: If x is '0101' and y is '010101', then I(x:y) ≈ 4 because knowing x lets you reconstruct y with little extra info.

concepts.name: Common Information
concepts.definition: The minimal amount of information needed to reconstruct two strings x and y together — formalized as the shortest program that can generate both.
concepts.intuition: Like giving two friends a single instruction manual to build their own identical LEGO models — the shared instructions are common information.
concepts.importance: Generalizes mutual information and enables analysis of joint structure in algorithmic data.
concepts.example: If x and y are both copies of the same file, common information equals C(x) = C(y), since one program generates both.

concepts.name: Information Distance
concepts.definition: A metric between two strings defined as the length of the shortest program that transforms one string into the other.
concepts.intuition: Like measuring how many edits you need to turn one document into another — but in terms of program steps, not characters.
concepts.importance: Provides a universal measure of similarity between objects independent of domain or representation.
concepts.example: The distance between '01' and '10' is small — a simple program flips the bits; distance between random strings is large.

concepts.name: Non-Shannon Inequalities
concepts.definition: Information-theoretic inequalities that hold for Kolmogorov complexity but not for Shannon entropy, revealing deeper structural constraints.
concepts.intuition: Like discovering new rules of arithmetic that don’t apply to basic addition — Kolmogorov complexity has hidden algebraic structure.
concepts.importance: Proves that algorithmic information behaves differently from classical probability-based information — a fundamental insight.
concepts.example: In Kolmogorov complexity, I(x:y) + I(x:z) ≤ I(x:y,z) + O(log n), a constraint that fails in Shannon entropy.

concepts.name: Effective Hausdorff Dimension
concepts.definition: A measure of the density of information in an infinite sequence, defined as the infimum over all effective Hausdorff measures for which the sequence is not null.
concepts.intuition: Think of it as how 'dense' or 'chaotic' the bits are — 1 means fully random, 0 means completely predictable.
concepts.importance: Generalizes randomness to quantify partial randomness — useful in analyzing fractal-like data and non-random sequences.
concepts.example: A sequence with alternating 0s and 1s has effective Hausdorff dimension 0.5 — it’s structured but not fully compressible.
